en: Itivuttaka 87: Tikanipāta, Catutthavagga (The Fourth Chapter) Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, when the venerable Ānanda knew that the Blessed One had risen from his seat and entered his dwelling, he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Bhante, it is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! How well-spoken were these words by the Blessed One: ‘One who does not know and see the Dhamma as it really is, is called an “unwise person” in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Now, Bhante, how is it that one who does not know and see the Dhamma as it really is, is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya? “Ānanda, one who does not know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering’—he is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who does not know and see as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—he is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who does not know and see as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—he is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who does not know and see as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—he is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Ānanda, one who knows and sees as it really is: ‘This is suffering’—he is called a ‘wise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who knows and sees as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’—he is called a ‘wise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who knows and sees as it really is:

‘This is the cessation of suffering’—he is called a ‘wise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. One who knows and sees as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—he is called a ‘wise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Bhante, it is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! How well-spoken were these words by the Blessed One: ‘One who does not know and see the Dhamma as it really is, is called an “unwise person” in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Bhante, those ascetics and brahmins who do not know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are unwise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. But those ascetics and brahmins who know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are wise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Indeed, Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins who do not know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are unwise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. And those ascetics and brahmins who know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are wise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the venerable Ānanda, having understood the meaning of what the Blessed One had said, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed for the village of Icchānaṅgala. There, the venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda. Then the venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, it is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends! How well-spoken were these words by the Blessed One: ‘One who does not know and see the Dhamma as it really is, is called an “unwise person” in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Now, friends, how is it that one who does not know and see the Dhamma as it really is, is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya? “Friends, one who does not know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering’—he is called an ‘unwise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya... [as above] ...he is called a ‘wise person’ in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. “Indeed, friends, those ascetics and brahmins who do not know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are unwise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. But those ascetics and brahmins who know and see as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they are wise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. When this was said, the bhikkhus said this to the venerable Ānanda: “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda! It is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well-spoken were these words by the venerable Ānanda: ‘Indeed, friends, those ascetics and brahmins who do not know and see as it really is... they are wise persons in the Noble Dhamma-Vinaya. Thus spoke the venerable Ānanda. Those bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in what the venerable Ānanda had said. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala, in the mango grove of Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, what is the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing? It is this: ‘This is suffering’; ‘This is the origin of suffering’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; it reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. “Bhikkhus, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of suffering. “What, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering. “And what, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has thus seen as it really is with correct wisdom, his mind becomes dispassionate towards the form element; his mind becomes dispassionate towards the feeling element; his mind becomes dispassionate towards the perception element; his mind becomes dispassionate towards
The *Andhakaraṇa Sutta*.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts that cause blindness, cause loss of vision, cause lack of knowledge, obstruct wisdom, belong to the side of affliction, and do not lead to Nibbāna."
Which three?
Sensual thought, bhikkhus, is blinding, it makes one sightless, it causes lack of knowledge, it obstructs wisdom, it belongs to the side of affliction, and it does not lead to Nibbāna.
Thought of ill will, bhikkhus, is blinding, it makes one sightless, it causes lack of knowledge, it obstructs wisdom, it belongs to the side of affliction, and it does not lead to Nibbāna.
“Bhikkhus, the thought of cruelty makes for blindness, makes for lack of vision, makes for lack of knowledge; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.

These, bhikkhus, are the three unwholesome thoughts that make for blindness, make for lack of vision, make for lack of knowledge; they obstruct wisdom, belong to the side of affliction, and do not lead to Nibbāna.

“There are, bhikkhus, these three wholesome thoughts that do not make for blindness, make for vision, make for knowledge; they increase wisdom, belong to the side of non-affliction, and lead to Nibbāna.”
Which three?
The thought of renunciation, monks, does not produce blindness; it produces vision, it produces knowledge, it increases wisdom, it belongs to the side of non-affliction, and it leads to Nibbāna.
The thought of non-ill will, monks, does not produce blindness; it produces vision, it produces knowledge, it increases wisdom, it belongs to the side of non-affliction, and it leads to Nibbāna.

“Bhikkhus, a thought of non-harming, bhikkhus, does not cause blindness; it provides vision, it provides knowledge, it increases wisdom, it belongs to the side of non-affliction, and it leads to Nibbāna.

These, bhikkhus, are the three wholesome thoughts that do not cause blindness, that provide vision, that provide knowledge, that increase wisdom, that belong to the side of non-affliction, and that lead to Nibbāna.
Thus the Blessed One spoke this matter.
In this regard, it is said:
“One should cultivate three types of wholesome thoughts,
And one should abandon three types that are unwholesome.”
He indeed calms his applied and sustained thoughts,
just as rain settles settled dust;
with a mind in which discursive thought has been stilled, he truly [attains peace].
“Right here he has attained the state of peace.
This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The eighth [sutta].
